characters.name: The Song of the Bow (Lament for Saul and Jonathan)
characters.purpose: A formal elegy David composes and orders taught to the men of Judah ("he bade them teach the children of Judah [the use of] the bow: behold, it is written in the book of Jasher," 2 Sam 1:18) for Saul and Jonathan after their deaths at Gilboa. Models honoring a fallen king and covenant-friend despite personal enmity/rivalry, and formal, preserved public mourning rather than private grief alone. (Attribution: David (composed the lament himself; ordered it taught to Judah))

verses.note: An Amalekite brings David Saul's crown and bracelet, claiming (falsely, per his own story) to have killed Saul at Saul's request; David has him executed on the strength of his own testimony.
David's lament, including the refrain "How are the mighty fallen," for both Saul and Jonathan, praising Jonathan's love as "passing the love of women" (v.26).

funFacts: The lament's instruction that it be taught and preserved in "the book of Jasher" (a now-lost source cited elsewhere in scripture, e.g. Joshua 10:13) is itself a rare KJV cross-reference to an external text.

characters.name: The Amalekite Messenger

genealogy.note: Unnamed; identifies himself only as "a young man... the son of a stranger, an Amalekite" (2 Sam 1:13).

verses.note: Reports Saul's death, presents the crown and bracelet, claims to have killed Saul; David judges him by his own confession ("thy blood be upon thy head; for thy mouth hath testified against thee," v.16) and has him killed.

funFacts: His account of killing Saul contradicts 1 Samuel 31:4-5, where Saul falls on his own sword — the text never resolves whether the Amalekite's story was true or an opportunistic lie; David executes him for claiming to have killed "the LORD's anointed" either way.

characters.name: David

genealogy.note: Father Jesse is established in 1 Samuel and not re-narrated in 2 Samuel itself; David's mother is never named in scripture. Additional wives Haggith, Abital, and Eglah (2 Sam 3:4-5) and further Hebron/Jerusalem-born sons are bulk-listed in genealogyLists, not repeated here since the text gives them no individual action in this book.

ageEvents.event: Began to reign (over Judah at Hebron); reigned 40 years total (7.5 in Hebron, 33 in Jerusalem)

verses.note: Anointed king over the house of Judah at Hebron.
Anointed king over all Israel; reigns 40 years.
Captures Jerusalem (Zion) from the Jebusites, makes it his city.
Brings the ark of God to Jerusalem; dances before it; Uzzah dies touching it en route (see uzzah); Michal despises him for dancing.
Orders a census against Joab's objection; a plague follows; buys Araunah's threshingfloor as an altar site (see threshingfloor_altar).

funFacts: David's wife Abigail (2 Sam 3:3, formerly Nabal's widow) is a different woman from Amasa's mother Abigail, David's own sister (2 Sam 17:25) — see abigail_davids_wife and amasa.
One of David's own sons born in Jerusalem is named Nathan (2 Sam 5:14) — a different person from Nathan the prophet (2 Sam 7, 12) — see nathan.

characters.name: Michal
characters.perkNote: Openly despises David's public dancing before the ark and confronts him for it (2 Sam 6:16-23) — an oppositional, not supportive, family role.

genealogy.note: Briefly given by Saul to Phaltiel (Palti) son of Laish before being reclaimed by David (2 Sam 3:14-16); 2 Sam 6:23 states plainly she "had no child unto the day of her death."

verses.note: David demands her return from Phaltiel as a condition of alliance with Abner.
Despises David dancing before the ark; rebukes him; the text notes she remained childless.

funFacts: 2 Samuel 21:8 (KJV) names "the five sons of Michal the daughter of Saul, whom she brought up for Adriel" — apparently in tension with 6:23's statement that Michal had no child, and with 1 Samuel 18:19, where it is Merab (Saul's older daughter), not Michal, who was given to Adriel the Meholathite. This is a well-known, unresolved textual crux (some manuscripts/translations read "Merab"); flagged, not silently resolved here.

characters.name: Ahinoam the Jezreelitess
characters.perkNote: David's wife and mother of his firstborn, Amnon.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

verses.note: Named as David's wife and mother of Amnon, his firstborn, born at Hebron.

funFacts: A different woman from "Ahinoam the daughter of Ahimaaz," Saul's own wife (1 Samuel 14:50) — two different Ahinoams in the same narrow story world.

characters.name: Abigail (David's wife, formerly Nabal's widow)
characters.perkNote: David's wife (widow of Nabal the Carmelite, per 1 Samuel 25) and mother of his son Chileab.

genealogy.note: Mother of Chileab (2 Sam 3:3); 1 Chronicles 3:1 gives this son's name as Daniel instead — a naming variant depending on a different, unstated book, hedged rather than merged here.

verses.note: Named as David's wife (formerly Nabal's wife) and mother of Chileab, born at Hebron.

funFacts: This is a DIFFERENT Abigail from Amasa's mother, Abigail, who is called David's own sister ("sister to Zeruiah," 2 Sam 17:25) — two distinct women named Abigail within David's own household/family, not the same person. See amasa.

characters.name: Maacah
characters.perkNote: David's wife, mother of Absalom and Tamar.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

verses.note: Named as daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, David's wife, and mother of Absalom, born at Hebron.

funFacts: "Maachah" is a name reused elsewhere in scripture for other, unrelated figures (e.g. a later queen mother in Judah's royal line) — flagged as a repeat name, not assumed to be the same person anywhere else it appears.

characters.name: Uzzah

genealogy.note: Brother of Ahio (2 Sam 6:3-4).

verses.note: Drives the cart carrying the ark; puts out his hand to steady it when the oxen stumble; struck dead by God for touching it.

funFacts: This Abinadab (Uzzah's father, in whose house the ark had rested) is a different person from Abinadab, Saul's son who died with him at Gilboa (1 Sam 31:2) — a repeat name to flag.

genealogy.note: Called Saul's kinsman; the exact degree (uncle vs. cousin) depends on how 1 Samuel's Ner/Kish genealogy (1 Sam 14:50-51) is read, which 2 Samuel itself does not spell out — hedged rather than asserted.

verses.note: Makes Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, king over Israel at Mahanaim after Saul's death.
Leads Ish-bosheth's forces against Joab's at Gibeon; kills Asahel in the retreat.
Quarrels with Ish-bosheth over Rizpah, defects to David, negotiates delivering all Israel to him.
Murdered by Joab at Hebron in revenge for Asahel, under pretense of a private word; David publicly mourns him and curses Joab's house.

genealogy.note: Also called Esh-baal elsewhere (1 Chron 8:33, 9:39) — a name variant from a different book, noted but not merged into this entry's primary name.

ageEvents.event: Began to reign over Israel (at Mahanaim); reigned two years

verses.note: Made king over Israel by Abner while David reigns only over Judah.
Accuses Abner of taking Rizpah, Saul's concubine; Abner reacts furiously and defects to David.
Assassinated in his bed by Rechab and Baanah, his own captains.

characters.name: Rechab and Baanah
characters.perkNote: Betray and kill their own king expecting reward from David.

genealogy.father: Rimmon the Beerothite (father of both, as brothers)
genealogy.note: The text does not differentiate the two brothers' individual actions — they act and are judged together, so they are kept as a single combined entry rather than split into two undifferentiated tiers.

verses.note: Captains of Ish-bosheth's raiding bands; kill him in his bed and bring his head to David, who instead has them executed and their bodies hung up for the murder of "a righteous person."

genealogy.note: Consistently called "Joab the son of Zeruiah" throughout 2 Samuel (e.g. 2:13, 3:39), which is stated directly in this book. That Zeruiah was David's own sister (making Joab David's nephew) is not stated in 2 Samuel itself — it depends on 1 Chronicles 2:16, a different book — hedged rather than asserted here.

verses.note: Commands David's forces at Gibeon against Abner; loses his brother Asahel in the fighting.
Rebukes David for sparing Abner, then kills Abner himself at the gate of Hebron in revenge for Asahel.
Commands the siege of Rabbah; carries out David's order to place Uriah where the fighting is fiercest so he will be killed.
Sends the wise woman of Tekoa to persuade David to allow Absalom's return from exile.
Personally kills Absalom, caught by his hair in a tree, against David's explicit order to deal gently with him.
Rebukes David for mourning Absalom over his living loyal soldiers.
Murders Amasa, David's newly appointed commander, by treachery at Gibeon.
Objects to David's census but carries it out; reports the numbered totals.

characters.name: Asahel
characters.perkNote: Joab's brother; his death at Abner's hand is the direct spark for Joab's later vengeance against Abner.

genealogy.note: Brother of Joab and Abishai.

verses.note: "Light of foot as a wild roe," pursues Abner in the retreat from Gibeon and is killed by him.

characters.name: Abishai
characters.perkNote: Joab's brother and constant second-in-command across the book's campaigns.

genealogy.note: Brother of Joab and Asahel.

verses.note: Offers to kill Shimei for cursing David; David restrains him.
Commands a third of David's army against Absalom's forces.
Marches with Joab against Sheba ben Bichri.
Chief among "the three mighty men" (a distinct rank from David's inner "three"); credited with killing 300 men with his spear.

funFacts: 2 Samuel 8:13 credits David with striking down 18,000 Edomites, while 1 Chronicles 18:12 attributes that same victory specifically to Abishai — a cross-book discrepancy noted, not resolved, here.

characters.name: The Davidic Covenant
characters.purpose: God's promise, delivered through Nathan, that David's house, kingdom, and throne will be established forever, and that David's son (not David himself) will build the temple. Establishes the theological foundation for an enduring royal dynastic line, later drawn on as a messianic hope, though 2 Samuel itself only records the promise, not its fulfillment. (Attribution: Nathan the prophet (relays the LORD's word to David))

verses.note: Nathan first tells David to do as he intends (build a temple), then relays God's overnight correction: David will not build the house, but God will build David a house (dynasty), and his son's throne will be established forever.
David's prayer of humble acceptance and thanks.

characters.name: Uriah the Hittite

genealogy.note: The child conceived during David's affair with Bathsheba was David's biological son, not Uriah's, despite the marriage — see bathsheba.

verses.note: Recalled from the siege of Rabbah by David; refuses to go home to his wife out of loyalty to his fellow soldiers and the ark while they are in the field, foiling David's attempt to cover the affair.
Sent back to the battle carrying his own death warrant; killed when Joab, on David's order, has him placed where the fighting is fiercest.
Listed among David's mighty men — the roster's closing name.

funFacts: Called "the Hittite" throughout, marking him as a non-Israelite serving loyally in David's elite guard.

characters.name: Bathsheba

genealogy.note: 2 Samuel 23:34 separately names "Eliam the son of Ahithophel" among David's mighty men. Whether this is the same Eliam who is Bathsheba's father — which would make her Ahithophel's granddaughter and offer a possible motive for Ahithophel's later betrayal of David — is never stated by the text itself; a plausible but unconfirmed inference, flagged rather than asserted.

verses.note: Seen bathing by David from the palace roof; sent for and lain with while Uriah is at war; conceives.
Mourns Uriah, then becomes David's wife; the first child dies as judgment (12:15-18).
Bears Solomon; the LORD loves him, and sends word by Nathan the prophet to name him Jedidiah.

funFacts: The first child of this union is never named in the text — he lives only seven days (2 Sam 12:18).

characters.name: Solomon (Jedidiah)
characters.perkNote: David and Bathsheba's son, given a second name by Nathan the prophet as a sign of God's favor.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given within 2 Samuel.

verses.note: Born to David and Bathsheba; named Jedidiah ("beloved of the LORD") by Nathan at God's instruction, alongside his given name Solomon.

funFacts: Not to be confused with David's other son also named Nathan (2 Sam 5:14), Solomon's own brother and a namesake of Nathan the prophet who named him.

characters.name: Nathan the Prophet

genealogy.note: No genealogy is given for Nathan himself in Samuel.

verses.note: Relays the Davidic Covenant to David (see davidic_covenant).
Personally confronts David after the Bathsheba/Uriah affair with the parable of the rich man's ewe lamb, pronounces judgment ("Thou art the man"), and receives David's confession of sin.
Sent by God to name the newborn Solomon "Jedidiah."

funFacts: At least two other, unrelated men named Nathan appear elsewhere in this book: David's own son (2 Sam 5:14) and "Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah," one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:36) — neither is this Nathan.

characters.name: Amnon

genealogy.note: David's firstborn son, born at Hebron.

verses.note: Feigns illness on his cousin Jonadab's advice to lure his half-sister Tamar to his house, then rapes her.
Immediately hates Tamar and has her thrown out.
Killed on Absalom's order at a sheep-shearing feast, two full years later, in revenge for Tamar.

funFacts: Amnon is Tamar's half-brother (different mother) but only Absalom's half-brother as well — Tamar and Absalom share their mother Maacah; Amnon does not.

characters.name: Tamar

genealogy.note: Full sister of Absalom (2 Sam 13:1); the text states she "remained desolate" in her brother Absalom's house afterward (13:20) and does not record her marrying.

verses.note: Sent by David to nurse the feigning-ill Amnon; raped by him despite her explicit protest and appeal to ask the king for her properly in marriage instead.
Puts ashes on her head, tears her garment, and mourns publicly; taken into Absalom's house.

funFacts: Absalom later names his own daughter Tamar as well (2 Samuel 14:27) — a second, different Tamar in the very same family within this book.

genealogy.note: 2 Samuel 14:27 states Absalom had three sons and one daughter, Tamar; 2 Samuel 18:18, however, has Absalom himself say "I have no son to keep my name in remembrance," prompting him to set up a monument for himself instead — a well-known internal tension the text does not reconcile (possibly the sons died young), hedged rather than resolved here.

verses.note: Avenges Tamar by having Amnon murdered at a feast; flees to his grandfather Talmai in Geshur for three years.
Recalled to Jerusalem through Joab's scheme with the wise woman of Tekoa, though kept from David's presence for two more years.
Wins the people's favor at the gate, then launches open rebellion from Hebron, drawing Ahithophel to his side.
On Ahithophel's advice, publicly lies with David's concubines on the palace roof.
Caught by his hair in an oak while fleeing on his mule; killed by Joab despite David's order to deal gently with him.
David's grief: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!"

characters.name: Hushai the Archite
characters.perkNote: David's friend, sent undercover into Absalom's court specifically to defeat Ahithophel's counsel.

genealogy.note: No genealogy given.

verses.note: David sends him back to Jerusalem to feign loyalty to Absalom and "defeat the counsel of Ahithophel."

Persuades Absalom to reject Ahithophel's fast-strike plan in favor of a slower muster, buying David time to escape; the text explicitly states the LORD determined to defeat Ahithophel's good counsel to bring evil upon Absalom.

characters.name: Ahithophel

genealogy.note: "Ahithophel the Gilonite" (2 Sam 15:12). 2 Samuel 23:34 names "Eliam the son of Ahithophel" among David's mighty men — possibly this Ahithophel's son, and possibly the same Eliam who is Bathsheba's father (see bathsheba), which would make Ahithophel her grandfather. Neither link is stated outright in the text; both are flagged as plausible but unconfirmed.

verses.note: David's counselor, joins Absalom's conspiracy at Giloh; his counsel "was as if a man had enquired at the oracle of God."
Advises Absalom to lie with David's concubines publicly, and (17:1-4) to strike David immediately with 12,000 men.
His advice is rejected in favor of Hushai's; seeing this, he sets his house in order and hangs himself.

funFacts: His possible family tie to Bathsheba (above) is worth flagging every time his motive for betraying David is discussed, since the text itself never states it.

characters.name: The Wise Woman of Tekoa
characters.perkNote: Acts as Joab's agent to maneuver David into recalling Absalom.

genealogy.note: Unnamed.

verses.note: Presents a fictional legal case (a feuding-sons parable) to David at Joab's direction, drawing him into a ruling that he then applies to Absalom's own exile.

characters.name: Shimei son of Gera
characters.perkNote: Publicly curses and throws stones at David during his flight from Absalom — direct, personal opposition.

genealogy.note: "Of the family of the house of Saul" (2 Sam 16:5).

verses.note: Curses David as a "man of Belial" and "bloody man," throwing stones and dust; David restrains Abishai from killing him.
Begs David's forgiveness on his return after Absalom's defeat; David swears not to kill him (though this is later revisited in 1 Kings 2, outside this book).

funFacts: "Shimei" is a very common name in scripture (e.g. a Levite, and others), so this Shimei son of Gera should not be assumed identical to any other Shimei encountered elsewhere.

characters.name: Mephibosheth (son of Jonathan)

genealogy.note: Lamed in both feet at age five when his nurse dropped him while fleeing news of Saul and Jonathan's deaths (2 Sam 4:4).

verses.note: Introduced: lamed in both feet from a childhood fall.
Sought out and shown kindness by David for Jonathan's sake; restored Saul's land and given a permanent place at the king's table.
His servant Ziba tells David (during Absalom's revolt) that Mephibosheth stayed behind hoping to reclaim Saul's kingdom; David gives Ziba all his land on the strength of this claim.

On David's return, disputes Ziba's account, claiming Ziba deceived him and slandered him; David splits the land between them rather than ruling definitively — the text never states which account was true.

funFacts: CRITICAL naming collision: a completely different person, also named Mephibosheth, appears later in this same book — one of Rizpah's two sons by Saul, handed over to the Gibeonites and executed (2 Sam 21:8). The two Mephibosheths are unrelated in role: this one is Jonathan's son, shown mercy by David; the other is Saul's grandson by a concubine, put to death. See rizpah.

characters.name: Ziba
characters.perkNote: A former servant of Saul's house assigned to serve Mephibosheth; benefits materially by accusing his own master.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

verses.note: Identified by David as a former servant of Saul's house; put in charge of working Mephibosheth's restored land.
Meets David with provisions during the flight from Absalom and accuses Mephibosheth of disloyalty; rewarded with Mephibosheth's land.
His account is disputed by Mephibosheth on David's return; the text does not resolve whose version is accurate.

characters.name: Amasa

genealogy.father: Ithra the Israelite (2 Samuel 17:25, KJV) — called "Jether the Ishmeelite" in 1 Chronicles 2:17, a further unreconciled discrepancy in both the father's name and his stated nationality between the two accounts.
genealogy.note: 2 Samuel 17:25 calls Amasa's mother Abigail "sister to Zeruiah, Joab's mother," and specifically "daughter of Nahash" — NOT "daughter of Jesse." 1 Chronicles 2:16-17 separately identifies both Zeruiah and Abigail as sisters of David (daughters of Jesse), which would make Amasa and Joab first cousins through their mothers — but 2 Samuel itself never states this Jesse lineage, and its own "daughter of Nahash" detail is an unreconciled textual oddity. This relationship is hedged, not asserted as settled fact.

verses.note: Appointed captain of Absalom's army in Joab's place during the rebellion.
After the rebellion's collapse, David offers Amasa command of his own army in Joab's place, to win over the men who had followed Absalom.
Murdered by Joab at Gibeon, struck in the belly with a sword while Joab feigns a friendly greeting, during the pursuit of Sheba ben Bichri.

funFacts: This Abigail, Amasa's mother, is a DIFFERENT woman from David's own wife Abigail (formerly Nabal's widow, 2 Sam 3:3) — two distinct Abigails connected to David's household. See abigail_davids_wife.

Whether Amasa and Joab were literally first cousins depends on 1 Chronicles 2:16-17's "daughters of Jesse" claim, which 2 Samuel's own "daughter of Nahash" wording (17:25) does not confirm — flagged as an open textual crux, not resolved here.

genealogy.note: "A man of Belial," a Benjamite (2 Sam 20:1).

verses.note: Blows a trumpet and calls Israel away from David ("every man to his tents, O Israel"), leading a second major rebellion right after Absalom's.
Besieged by Joab at Abel of Beth-maachah; beheaded by the city's inhabitants at the wise woman of Abel's urging to end the siege.

characters.name: The Wise Woman of Abel
characters.perkNote: Negotiates directly with Joab to end his siege by having the rebel Sheba's head thrown over the wall instead.

genealogy.note: Unnamed.

verses.note: Calls out to Joab, negotiates the terms, persuades the city to kill Sheba and throw his head over the wall, ending the siege.

characters.name: Hanun

genealogy.note: Succeeds his father Nahash as king of the Ammonites.

verses.note: Shames David's messengers of condolence — shaving off half their beards and cutting their garments to the buttocks — on his princes' advice that they were spies; this insult ignites the Ammon/Aram war that occupies chapter 10 and sets up David remaining in Jerusalem in chapter 11.

funFacts: The war his insult starts is the direct backdrop for the Bathsheba affair: David "tarried still at Jerusalem" (11:1) while Joab besieged the Ammonite capital, Rabbah.

characters.name: Barzillai the Gileadite
characters.perkNote: A very aged, wealthy Gileadite who personally provisions David's camp during Absalom's rebellion.

genealogy.note: Whether Chimham, whom Barzillai asks David to take in his place, is literally his son is not stated outright in the text (2 Sam 19:37-38 has Barzillai simply say "let thy servant Chimham go over") — a common inference, hedged rather than asserted here.

verses.note: Brings beds, basins, food, and provisions to David's hungry, weary camp at Mahanaim, alongside Shobi son of Nahash and Machir son of Ammiel.
Escorts David partway back over the Jordan; declines David's offer of reward at court due to his old age ("I am this day fourscore years old"), asking that Chimham go in his place instead.

characters.name: The Gibeonite Reckoning
characters.purpose: A three-year famine is revealed to be judgment for Saul's earlier bloodguilt against the Gibeonites (violating Israel's centuries-old sworn oath to spare them, made back in Joshua's day). Addresses covenant-keeping and blood atonement — that an oath sworn in the LORD's name binds even later generations, and that unaddressed bloodguilt has national consequences. (Attribution: The Gibeonites (state the terms of atonement); the LORD (reveals the famine's cause to David))

verses.note: The LORD reveals the famine is "for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites"; the Gibeonites, when asked, request seven of Saul's male descendants be handed over rather than accepting silver or gold.
David hands over Armoni and Mephibosheth (Rizpah's sons by Saul) and five more descendants of Saul; they are hanged/put to death before the LORD, and the famine is later described as lifting.

characters.name: Rizpah

children: Mephibosheth (Rizpah's son, distinct from Jonathan's son)
genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

verses.note: Named as Saul's concubine; Abner's alleged relation with her sparks his break with Ish-bosheth.

Her two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, are among the seven descendants of Saul handed to the Gibeonites and killed; she spreads sackcloth on a rock and guards the exposed bodies from birds by day and beasts by night, from the start of harvest until rain finally falls.
Her vigil prompts David to retrieve Saul and Jonathan's bones as well and give all of them proper burial together.

funFacts: Her son here, named Mephibosheth, is a DIFFERENT person from Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan (chapters 4, 9, 16, 19) — Saul had two grandsons who shared this exact name through different lines. See mephibosheth_jonathans_son for the other one.

characters.name: The Mighty Men
characters.purpose: A formal, named honor-roll of David's elite warriors and their individual feats, closing out the book's account of his reign. Exists to preserve individual valor and loyalty within the king's inner circle by name, not to advance plot on its own. (Attribution: The closing roster appended to David's own words (2 Samuel 23:8-39))

verses.note: Adino (Josheb-basshebeth) the Tachmonite, chief of the captains, credited with killing 800 men at one time.
Eleazar son of Dodo stands his ground alone against the Philistines when the other men withdraw, until his hand "clave unto the sword."
Shammah son of Agee defends a plot of lentiles alone against a Philistine troop.

Three of the thirty break through Philistine lines to draw water from the well of Bethlehem for David, who refuses to drink it and pours it out to the LORD instead, calling it too costly ("the blood of the men that went in jeopardy of their lives").
Benaiah son of Jehoiada — slew two lionlike men of Moab, killed a lion in a pit on a day of snow, and killed a huge Egyptian, taking the Egyptian's own spear from his hand; set over David's guard.

funFacts: Uriah the Hittite (see uriah) appears as the roster's final name (23:39), tying this list back to the Bathsheba narrative.

genealogy.note: No further genealogy given.

verses.note: Individually distinguished among the mighty men: kills two lionlike men of Moab, kills a lion in a pit in time of snow, and kills a heavily armed Egyptian with the Egyptian's own spear; set by David over his personal guard.

characters.name: The Threshingfloor Altar
characters.purpose: After a census David takes against Joab's objection brings a plague as judgment, Gad the prophet gives David a choice of three punishments; once the plague is stayed, Gad instructs David to build an altar on Araunah's threshingfloor. Establishes the future Temple site (later built on this ground) and teaches that acceptable sacrifice must cost the giver something ("neither will I offer... of that which doth cost me nothing," 24:24). (Attribution: Gad the prophet (instructs David to build the altar); Araunah (offers the site))

verses.note: Gad presents David with three options (famine, fleeing enemies, or pestilence) as judgment for the census; David chooses to fall into the LORD's hand.
Gad instructs David to raise an altar on Araunah's threshingfloor; Araunah offers it and his oxen freely, but David insists on paying full price.

genealogy.note: Also spelled "Ornan" in 1 Chronicles 21 — a spelling/name variant from a different book, not a different person.

verses.note: Owns the threshingfloor David buys as an altar site; offers it, his oxen for sacrifice, and the threshing instruments for wood free of charge; David refuses, insisting on paying full price (fifty shekels of silver) rather than offering God something that cost him nothing.

genealogyLists.david_sons_born_at_hebron_2sam_3_2_5: Amnon (Ahinoam), Chileab/Daniel (Abigail), Absalom (Maacah), Adonijah (Haggith), Shephatiah (Abital), Ithream (Eglah) — only Amnon, Absalom, and (via Solomon's household) Adonijah have individual narrative action within 2 Samuel itself; Chileab, Shephatiah, and Ithream are bulk genealogy only.
genealogyLists.david_sons_born_at_jerusalem_2sam_5_14_1: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Elishama, Eliada, Eliphalet — bulk list; Solomon and the different Nathan are the only two with any individual mention elsewhere in the book.
genealogyLists.michal_merab_adriel_crux_2sam_21_8: 2 Samuel 21:8 (KJV) names "the five sons of Michal" given to Adriel the Meholathite, apparently conflicting with 6:23 (Michal had no child) and 1 Samuel 18:19 (it was Merab, Saul's other daughter, given to Adriel). Flagged as an unresolved textual crux rather than silently corrected.
genealogyLists.provisioners_of_davids_camp_2sam_17_27_2: Shobi son of Nahash of Rabbah, Machir son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite bring provisions to David at Mahanaim; only Barzillai has further individual action later in the book. Shobi's father Nahash may or may not be the same Nahash referenced regarding Amasa's mother Abigail (17:25) — an unresolved ambiguity, not asserted as the same person.
genealogyLists.amasa_nahash_ambiguity: 2 Samuel 17:25 calls Amasa's mother Abigail "daughter of Nahash," not "daughter of Jesse" — see amasa's genealogy note for the full hedge on this crux and its tension with 1 Chronicles 2:16-17.
genealogyLists.abiathar_ahimelech_crux: 2 Samuel 8:17 (KJV) itself reads "Ahimelech the son of Abiathar," reversing the father-son relationship given in 1 Samuel. Neither Abiathar nor Ahimelech was given an individual character entry in this book's roster (no differentiated action within 2 Samuel itself beyond the officials list, 8:16-18), so the crux is logged here rather than asserted via a standalone entry.
